She jumped out of a plane at 58

caption: Her daughter texted her the night before and said:

She did it anyway.

She had spent thirty years doing the reasonable thing. The safe thing. The age-appropriate thing. She raised three kids, held a career together, and somewhere in her late forties she started hearing herself say

before she had even decided whether she wanted to try.

At 58, she booked the jump.

Not because she was brave. Not because she had something to prove. She booked it because she realized she had been running a quiet, invisible calculation her entire adult life — what's allowed now versus what I used to be allowed to do — and nobody had ever told her who made that rule.

Free-fall lasts about sixty seconds.

She said the part that surprised her wasn't the drop. It was the moment before the door opened, when she realized the fear she was feeling was familiar. She had felt it before job changes, before moving cities, before every meaningful thing she had ever done. Fear didn't mean stop. It meant she was about to do something real.

She landed. She cried. She texted her daughter back:

The research on this is more consistent than people expect. Adults who take on new physical challenges in their fifties and sixties report stronger sense of identity, better emotional regulation, and significantly less dread about aging than those who stop. Not because the activity itself rewires the brain — but because the decision to try does.

The ceiling isn't the body. The ceiling is the story we've been telling about what the body is allowed to do.

Different place. Different routine. Middle-of-the-night wake-up. Comment CALM and I'll send you a free one-page phone guide with 4 simple steps to keep nearby.

You can also get it from the link in my bio.
